https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/ee_chip.3799adad529e08557a1b80925a68d3a69792192d965268d6e3973f43a039b827_hu_7e90bdee7c08a7ce.webp 800w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="800" height="678" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/ee_chip.3799adad529e08557a1b80925a68d3a69792192d965268d6e3973f43a039b827.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The Emotion Engine, as seen on the first motherboard revision of this console.</figcaption></figure><p>This chipset contains numerous components, one of them being the main CPU. The rest are at the CPU’s disposal to speed up certain tasks. For this analysis, we’ll divide the EE into three sections:</p><ul><li>The <strong>leader</strong>: The main component that controls the entire chip.</li><li>The <strong>memory available</strong>, a crucial ingredient so the processors can do meaningful operations.</li><li>The <strong>co-processors</strong>: These accelerate particular computations.</li></ul><h3 id="the-leader">The leader</h3><p>In a nutshell, the main CPU is a <strong>MIPS R5900</strong>, an exclusive MIPS core designed for this console. You may recall when Sony started <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#tab-1-2-mips-and-sony">venturing with MIPS silicon</a> with the very first <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/">PlayStation</a> (where we can find a <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#the-offering">MIPS R3000A</a> second sourced from LSI). For the next generation, we’ve got a MIPS ‘R5900’… but what does that name mean for us?</p><p>To understand what’s hidden behind the new numbers, let’s take a look at some history surrounding that era.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-1-1-outperforming-success-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-1-1-outperforming-success">Outperforming success</a></li><li id="tab-1-2-high-end-for-the-masses-link"><a href="#tab-1-2-high-end-for-the-masses">High-end for the masses</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-1-1-outperforming-success"><h4 id="tab-1-1-outperforming-success" class="tab-title">Outperforming success</h4><p>The <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#cpu">MIPS R4000</a> was a popular CPU series adopted by a wide range of systems, including a <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/">close competitor</a>. Thanks to its success, MIPS brought a once-unaffordable range of advancements (64-bit computing, 8-stage pipelines and so forth) to the masses.</p><p>Fast forward, the next big leap arrived in 1995, with the release of the <strong>R10000</strong>. Now under the funding of <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#tab-1-2-mips-and-sony">SGI</a>, MIPS produced a new processor that took the R4000’s parallelism capabilities miles further, debuting techniques like <sup id="bibref:3"><a href="#bib:cpu-yeager" role="doc-biblioref">[3]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li><strong>Speculative execution</strong>: The CPU predicts the result of conditional branches before they are computed. The predictions are based on previous results stored in an internal 512-entry table. Once the condition is computed, if the prediction turns out to be correct, the CPU has saved valuable time. Otherwise, the extra computations are discarded.<ul><li>Thanks to this, MIPS has finally turned a recurrent problem (<a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#delay-galore">control hazards</a>) into an advantage.</li><li>In other CPUs, you may find similar functionality referred to as <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#the-powerpc-gekko">dynamic branch prediction</a>.</li></ul></li><li><strong>4-issue superscalar</strong> pipeline: On top of the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/sega-saturn/#cpu">pipelined design</a>, the CPU will now fetch up to four instructions at the start of the pipeline, and distribute them across separate units, allowing the CPU to execute these instructions at the same time. In doing so, the CPU achieves a greater degree of parallelism.</li><li><strong>Out-of-order execution</strong>: The CPU will also re-arrange the sequence of instructions to try to fill up its units as much as possible (as long as no hazards are added).</li><li><strong>L2 cache with a 128-bit bus</strong>, enabling to pull more data into the CPU at a time, which becomes a requirement based on the previous enhancements.</li></ul><p>Such innovation came at the cost of a complex design, however, and the final product was everything but cheap. SGI only bundled it in high-end equipment, and any attempt to bring it into a home console was out of the question.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-2-high-end-for-the-masses">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-2-high-end-for-the-masses"><h4 id="tab-1-2-high-end-for-the-masses" class="tab-title">High-end for the masses</h4><p>Already aware of the commercial limitations of the R10000, SGI/MIPS hired <strong>Quantum Effect Devices</strong> (QED) to develop an affordable version of the R10000 for the mid-to-low-end market. As a company founded by former MIPS employees, QED was in the business of designing variants of MIPS cores for the budget sector.</p><p>In the end, QED came back with a new core called the <strong>R5000</strong>, this was an R10000 that underwent significant cutbacks <sup id="bibref:4"><a href="#bib:cpu-halfhill" role="doc-biblioref">[4]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li>Out-of-order execution is reverted to in-order.</li><li>Speculative execution is removed.</li><li>Superscalability is limited to two instructions (2-issue) and doesn’t parallelise integer instructions anymore. However, floating point instructions can still be paired with others.</li><li>Due to the previous reductions, L2 is scaled down to a 64-bit bus instead.</li></ul><p>Consequently, this became an ideal CPU to power economical equipment, such as SGI’s low-end workstations. In any case, notice that the cut-down pipeline still performed concurrent floating-point operations, as if QED planned to keep it an attractive product for <strong>vector/3D applications</strong>. You’ll soon see that another company quickly took note of that as well.</p><p>As a side note, it’s curious to observe that on the other side of the pond, there were similar advancements but in the opposite direction: <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-ds/#arms-new-territories">ARM joined forces with DEC</a> in the pursuit of lifting ARM chips into the high-end market.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-1-outperforming-success">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h4 id="a-special-order-for-sony">A special order for Sony</h4><p>Toshiba had been a MIPS licensee for some time <sup id="bibref:5"><a href="#bib:cpu-toshiba" role="doc-biblioref">[5]</a></sup> and was no stranger to manufacturing MIPS variations and packages. At one point, Sony and Toshiba joined forces to produce a CPU exclusively tailored for Sony’s upcoming console. This was a tremendous benefit for Toshiba: very often CPUs are required to fulfill a wide range of requirements coming from different stakeholders, and in doing so it constraints opportunities for specialisation. Now, there was only a single purpose: <strong>3D gaming</strong>. Thus, granting enough room for all kinds of <strong>innovation</strong>.</p><p>That being said, Toshiba ended up grabbing the affordable R5000 design and tweaked it to accelerate vector operations. The new core is called <strong>R5900</strong> and debuts the following ‘3D’ enhancements <sup id="bibref:6"><a href="#bib:cpu-stokes" role="doc-biblioref">[6]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li>A variation of the <strong>MIPS III ISA</strong>. This includes the original 64-bit ISA previously seen on the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#cpu">Nintendo 64</a>, but extended with interesting opcodes. Sony added some instructions from <strong>MIPS IV</strong> (prefetch and conditional move) along with their own SIMD extension called <strong>multimedia instructions</strong> to accelerate vector calculations (similar to the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/dreamcast/#special-work">SH-4</a>, but integer only).<ul><li>The multimedia instructions are still 32-bit wide but can operate up to three 128-bit vectors at a time. They offer operations such as vector arithmetic, min/max and many kinds of scalar combinations to form new vectors.</li></ul></li><li><strong>32 128-bit general-purpose registers</strong>: Another significant Toshiba-branded enhancement. Forget about the typical <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#the-offering">32-bit storage</a>, we’ve stepped into the 128-bit realm now. Nevertheless, the majority of operations will hardly use all the available space (MIPS words are <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#cpu">still 64-bit long</a>). This is when the aforementioned multimedia extension comes into the equation, as its set will make full utilisation of the extended register file.<ul><li>When using the new instructions, each register can store vectors made of many types of scalars (from two 64-bit integers to sixteen 8-bit ones).</li><li>To prevent performance penalties, these registers are accessed through a <strong>128-bit bus</strong>, while the rest of the CPU uses an internal <strong>64-bit data bus</strong>.</li></ul></li><li>Two <strong>64-bit ALUs</strong>. Each can operate 64-bit integers independently, but also combine to become a <strong>128-bit ALU</strong>. The latter is the brain behind those shiny multimedia opcodes.</li></ul><p>Aside from these, we also find other improvements that developers may welcome as well:</p><ul><li><strong>6-stage pipeline</strong>: That’s one additional stage compared to <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#the-offering">the predecessors</a>.</li><li><strong>2-way superscalar</strong> execution: Thanks to the two ALUs, up to two 64-bit integer operations are now executed in parallel.<ul><li>This restores another lost advantage of the MIPS R10000.</li></ul></li><li><strong>24 KB L1 cache</strong>: Divided into <strong>16 KB for instructions</strong> and <strong>8 KB for data</strong>.<ul><li>The circuitry also implements a <strong>prefetch function</strong> to cache instructions and data before they are requested. This is done by including extra logic that can identify which places in memory are more often requested.</li></ul></li><li><strong>16 KB of Scratchpad RAM</strong>, also known as ‘Fast RAM’.</li><li><strong>Memory management unit</strong>: Interfaces memory access with the rest of the system.</li></ul><p>Moreover, the core is complemented with a <strong>dedicated floating point unit</strong> (identified as ‘COP1’) that accelerates operations with 32-bit floating-point numbers (also known as <code>floats</code> in C). This is a peculiar block as it <strong>doesn’t follow the IEEE 754 standard</strong>, most evident with its absence of <code>infinity</code> (computed as <code>0</code> instead) <sup id="bibref:7"><a href="#bib:cpu-krysto" role="doc-biblioref">[7]</a></sup>. Apart from that, it features 32 32-bit registers.</p><h3 id="a-recognisable-memory-choice">A recognisable memory choice</h3><p>Next to the Emotion Engine are two blocks of 16 MB of RAM, giving a total of <strong>32 MB</strong> of main memory. The type of memory used is <strong>RDRAM</strong> (<a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#memory-design">déjà vu!</a>) which is accessed through a <strong>16-bit bus</strong>.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/memoryarch.ef03a684eae05160a0996b02f1ec35914ed0fdb3a44653fdd07b5af37904100d.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="637" height="308" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/memoryarch.ef03a684eae05160a0996b02f1ec35914ed0fdb3a44653fdd07b5af37904100d.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Memory design of the Emotion Engine. You can guess where the congestion will emerge.</figcaption></figure><p>At first, this can be a little disappointing to hear, considering the internal bus of the Emotion engine is as wide as 128 bits. However, the RAM chips are strategically placed by following the <strong>dual-channel architecture</strong>, which consists of connecting both chips using two independent 16-bit buses (one bus per chip) to improve data throughput. The resulting setup provides a theoretical 3.2 GB/sec, so rest assured that memory latency is not an issue in this console!</p><p>At one corner of the Emotion engine there is a powerful <strong>DMA Controller</strong> or ‘DMAC’ that transfers data between main memory and Scratchpad; or between main memory and any component inside the EE.</p><p>Data transfers are done in batches of 128 bits, but here is the interesting part: Every eight batches, the main bus is temporarily unlocked. This leaves a small window to perform other DMA transfers in parallel (up to ten) or let the CPU use the main bus. This <em>modus operandi</em> is called <strong>slice mode</strong> and is one of the many modes available on this DMA unit. Bear in mind that while slice mode reduces stalls on the main bus, it does so at the cost of slowing down the overall DMA transfer.</p><h3 id="preventing-past-mishaps">Preventing past mishaps</h3><p>Whether we want it or not, with the amount of traffic happening inside the Emotion Engine, this design will eventually suffer the consequences of the <strong>Unified memory architecture</strong> or ‘UMA’. That is: multiple independent components trying to access main memory at the same time, causing congestion. Well, to correct these issues, Sony alleviated the constant need for memory by:</p><ul><li>Wrapping their processors with <strong>lots of cache</strong>. Thus, only requiring access to main memory if it’s absolutely necessary.<ul><li>99% of cache/scratchpad mentions in this article will be for this reason.</li></ul></li><li>Adding a 128-byte <strong>Write Back Buffer</strong>: Very similar to the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#ibms-enhancements">Write Gather Pipe</a>, but instead of waiting until it’s 25% full, it will check the state of the bus (i.e. congested or free) first.</li></ul><p>This sounds very convenient for applications that can benefit from cache, but what about those tasks, such as manipulating Display Lists, which shouldn’t use cache at all? Luckily, the CPU provides a different memory access mode called <strong>UnCached</strong>, which <strong>only</strong> uses the Write Back Buffer. Thus, it will not waste cycles correcting the cache (product of <em>cache misses</em>).</p><p>Furthermore, the <strong>UnCached accelerated mode</strong> is also available. This one adds a buffer for speeding up the reading of continuous addresses in memory.</p><h3 id="other-interesting-bits">Other interesting bits</h3><p>Inside the same Emotion Engine package, there is yet another processor called <strong>Image Processing Unit</strong> or ‘IPU’, this time designed for <strong>image decompression</strong>. As the successor of the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#tab-2-3-motion-decoder">MDEC</a>, the IPU can be useful when a game needs to decode an MPEG2 movie without jamming the main CPU.</p><p>Long story short, the game sends compressed image streams to the IPU (hopefully using DMA) which are then decoded in a format that the GPU can display. The PS2’s operating system also relies on the IPU to provide DVD playback.</p><p>Finally, the IPU also operates compressed <strong>High-resolution textures</strong>, which saves CPU usage and reduces large transfers.</p><hr><h2 id="co-cpus">Co CPUs</h2><p>It’s been two years since the rivals presented their <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/dreamcast/">latest offering</a>. If you read the former article and just started reading this one, I presume you are <em>still</em> waiting for ‘the thing’ that makes the PS2 as powerful as it seemed back then. Now, let me introduce a <em>very</em> important set of components Sony fitted in the Emotion Engine, the <strong>Vector Processing Units</strong> or ‘VPU’.</p><h3 id="architecture">Architecture</h3><p>A Vector Processing Unit is a small independent processor designed to operate vectors, in particular, vectors made of four <code>floats</code>. These processors are so fast that they only spend <strong>one cycle per operation</strong>, which can be extremely convenient for geometry processing. Though they exhibit similar unstandardised behaviour to the CPU’s FPU.</p><p>VPUs are made of the following components:</p><ul><li>Some <strong>Vector Unit Memory</strong> or ‘VU Mem’: Used as a working space for the Vector unit. It stores values needed to be operated and/or the results of previous operations.</li><li>A <strong>Vector Unit</strong>: The core of the processor. It contains some memory (called <strong>Micro Memory</strong>) to store a program (called <strong>Microprogram</strong>) which instructs the unit on how to operate the data found in ‘VU Mem’.<ul><li>It implements a <strong>64-bit ISA</strong> and the execution unit is <strong>split into two parallel sub-units</strong>. The first one multiplies or adds floats, while the other one divides floats or operates integers. This enables to operate both floats and integers <strong>concurrently</strong>.</li></ul></li><li>A <strong>Vector Interface</strong>: Automatically decompresses vertex data coming from main memory in a format the Vector unit can understand. This unit can also transfer microprograms to Micro Memory.</li></ul><h3 id="functionality">Functionality</h3><p>To start working, the vector unit needs to be ‘kickstarted’. For this, the main CPU is in charge of supplying the microcode.</p><p>There are <strong>two VPUs</strong> fitted in the Emotion engine, but they are arranged differently, giving way to different uses and optimisations.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-2-1-vector-processing-unit-0-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-2-1-vector-processing-unit-0">Vector Processing Unit 0</a></li><li id="tab-2-2-vector-processing-unit-1-link"><a href="#tab-2-2-vector-processing-unit-1">Vector Processing Unit 1</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-2-1-vector-processing-unit-0"><h4 id="tab-2-1-vector-processing-unit-0" class="tab-title">Vector Processing Unit 0</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/vpu0.22473bdba559fbcb674ee36a985104d23e1320ddc06b930d49a0117150c54bf2.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="927" height="481" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/vpu0.22473bdba559fbcb674ee36a985104d23e1320ddc06b930d49a0117150c54bf2.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Architecture of VPU0.</figcaption></figure><p>The first VPU, the <strong>VPU0</strong>, is positioned between the CPU and the other vector unit (VPU1). It provides an ‘assisting’ role to the main CPU.</p><p>The VPU0 has two modes of operation:</p><ul><li><strong>Micromode</strong>: This is the ‘traditional mode’. The VPU will independently execute ‘microinstructions’ from a microprogram stored in Micro memory.</li><li><strong>Macromode</strong>: The VPU0 becomes the ‘COP2’ of the main CPU and executes ‘macro-instructions’, received from the main CPU through a dedicated 128-bit bus.<ul><li>Macro-instructions have the same functionality as microinstructions but use different opcodes. Nonetheless, the VPU execution unit is no longer split (meaning it can only execute one instruction at a time).</li><li>While this mode doesn’t make full utilisation of all the components of the VPU0, it still speeds up the CPU’s vector operations. Moreover, in terms of simplicity, a co-processor is easier to program than an independent unit (something PC programmers will find helpful).</li></ul></li></ul><p>The memory map of the VPU0 also has access to some of the other VPU’s registers and flags, presumably to check its state or quickly read the results of some operations done by the other VPU.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-2-vector-processing-unit-1">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-2-vector-processing-unit-1"><h4 id="tab-2-2-vector-processing-unit-1" class="tab-title">Vector Processing Unit 1</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/vpu1.23022615284ce6b896b02d835b5048165c133b900431eb1fa4c23ea3abc3700b.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="864" height="481" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/vpu1.23022615284ce6b896b02d835b5048165c133b900431eb1fa4c23ea3abc3700b.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Architecture of VPU1.</figcaption></figure><p>The second VPU found, the <strong>VPU1</strong>, is an enhanced version of the VPU0 with quadruple the amount of micro memory and VU memory. Moreover, this unit includes an additional component called <strong>Elementary function unit</strong> or ‘EFU’ which speeds up the execution of exponential and trigonometric functions.</p><p>The VPU1 is located between the VPU0 and the Graphics Interface (the ‘gate’ to the GPU), so it includes additional buses to feed the geometry to the GPU as quickly as possible and without using the main bus.</p><p>On the other side and due to its location, the VPU1 <strong>only operates in micromode</strong>.</p><p>It’s obvious that this VPU was designed for trigonometric operations, and may serve as a pre-processor for the GPU. Hence, it’s often put in charge of delivering the famous Display Lists.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-1-vector-processing-unit-0">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="infinite-worlds">Infinite worlds</h3><p>A useful approach that can be exploited with these units is <strong>procedural generation</strong>. In other words, instead of building the scene using hard-coded geometry, let the VPUs generate it using algorithms. In this case, the VPU computes <strong>mathematical functions to produce the geometry</strong> which is then interpreted by the GPU (i.e. triangles, lines, quadrangles, etc) and ultimately used to draw the scene.</p><p>Compared to using explicit data, procedural content is ideal for parallelised tasks, it frees up bandwidth, requires very little storage and it’s dynamic (programmers can set parameters to achieve different results) <sup id="bibref:8"><a href="#bib:cpu-green" role="doc-biblioref">[8]</a></sup>. Many areas can highly benefit from this technique:</p><ul><li><strong>Complex surfaces</strong> (e.g. spheres and wheels).</li><li><strong>World rendering</strong> (e.g. terrains, particles, trees).</li><li><strong>Bézier curves</strong>, a very popular equation in computer graphics used to draw curves. These are turned into a <strong>Bézier patch</strong> (explicit geometry) and support different degrees of precision based on the level of detail required.</li></ul><p>On the other side, procedural content may struggle with animations and, if the algorithm is too complex, the VPU might not generate the geometry at the required time.</p><p>To sum up, procedural rendering is not a new technique, but thanks to the VPUs, it opens the doors to further optimisations and richer graphics. Nonetheless, is not a simple technique to implement and Sony R&D published various papers describing different approaches to use on their console <sup id="bibref:9"><a href="#bib:cpu-tumati" role="doc-biblioref">[9]</a></sup>.</p><h3 id="you-define-the-workflow">You define the workflow</h3><p>With these new additions, programmers now have a lot of flexibility to design their graphics engines. To assist with this, Sony spent additional resources to devise and document efficient pipeline designs. The following are examples of graphics pipelines optimised for different types of workloads <sup id="bibref:10"><a href="#bib:cpu-stokes" role="doc-biblioref">[10]</a></sup>:</p><div class="tabs nested centered-container"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-1-1-parallel-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-1-1-parallel">Parallel</a></li><li id="nestedtab-1-2-serial-link"><a href="#nestedtab-1-2-serial">Serial</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-1-1-parallel"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/programming/parallel.6387b0c6bbc9040ba0ebfde7bebf41d681eec2e2ff52db38b7b26163a919886b.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="620" height="321" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/programming/parallel.6387b0c6bbc9040ba0ebfde7bebf41d681eec2e2ff52db38b7b26163a919886b.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Parallel pipeline design.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-1-2-serial"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/programming/serial.e0c435db7dbf5e5850e1e31e5cef378e728e43cdeda8f468dbd9e9714aacb76e.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="833" height="202" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/programming/serial.e0c435db7dbf5e5850e1e31e5cef378e728e43cdeda8f468dbd9e9714aacb76e.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Serial pipeline design.</figcaption></figure></div><p>In the first example, the <strong>Parallel</strong> design, the CPU is combined with the VPU0 in macromode to produce geometry in parallel with the VPU1. The CPU/VPU0 group makes full utilisation of scratchpad and cache to avoid using the main bus, which the VPU1 relies on to fetch data from main memory. In the end, both rendering groups concurrently send their respective Display Lists to the GPU.</p><p>The second example, the <strong>Serial</strong> design, proposes a different approach where the CPU/VPU0 group works as a preprocessor for the VPU1. The first stage will fetch and process all the geometry that the VPU1 will subsequently turn into Display List.</p><p>These have been so far examples from the theoretical point of view, but to explain a more ‘practical’ implementation, I’m going to refer to a video Jon Burton published regarding the development of one of their PS2 games <sup id="bibref:11"><a href="#bib:cpu-burton" role="doc-biblioref">[11]</a></sup>.</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/Crash.75863381a688a9749a92f314a3a9c09c21e7849511d551517c0407e383458603.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/Crash.75863381a688a9749a92f314a3a9c09c21e7849511d551517c0407e383458603_hu_24a3af74ad6698f1.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/Crash.75863381a688a9749a92f314a3a9c09c21e7849511d551517c0407e383458603_hu_cfab775cc9751674.webp 640w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="640" height="448" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/Crash.75863381a688a9749a92f314a3a9c09c21e7849511d551517c0407e383458603.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Crash Bandicoot: The Wrath of Cortex (2001). Particles make the candle flame and the light coming from the window glass.</figcaption></figure><p>The former director of Travellers Tales explained how his team achieved a particle system fully encapsulated within the VPU1. In a nutshell, the VPU1 focused on reading a pre-populated database from its VU memory, the database was used to calculate the coordinates of particles at any given time without depending on any other component. The result of the operation could be transformed into Display Lists and sent right away.</p></div><p>With this approach, the CPU was significantly offloaded, allowing it to carry out other tasks like AI and physics.</p><p>There are many more examples out there, but to sum things up: It is now up to the programmer to find the optimal setup, and that, is a good thing.</p><hr><h2 id="graphics">Graphics</h2><p>Considering all the work done by the Emotion Engine, is there something left? The last step actually: Display!</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/ffx.db39ede71c910f7a403331b853775fa9e2c3801c8ed80be1c6adc67be1806263.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/ffx.db39ede71c910f7a403331b853775fa9e2c3801c8ed80be1c6adc67be1806263_hu_869c3c392f7b832a.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/ffx.db39ede71c910f7a403331b853775fa9e2c3801c8ed80be1c6adc67be1806263_hu_c11d225404751b46.webp 512w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="512" height="416" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/ffx.db39ede71c910f7a403331b853775fa9e2c3801c8ed80be1c6adc67be1806263.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Final Fantasy X (2001).</figcaption></figure><p>There’s a simple but speedy chip specialised in that: The <strong>Graphics Synthesizer</strong> or ‘GS’ running at <strong>~147.46 MHz</strong>. It contains <strong>4 MB of DRAM</strong> embedded inside to do all processing in-house. Thus, removing the need to access the main memory. The embedded RAM (eDRAM) is connected using different buses depending on the type of data needed.</p><p>The GS has fewer features than other graphics systems <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#graphics">previously reviewed</a> on this site. Nonetheless, it’s very fast at what it does.</p></div><h3 id="architecture-and-design">Architecture and design</h3><p>This GPU only does <strong>rasterisation</strong> and that is… Generating pixels, mapping textures, applying lighting and some other effects. This means there are no vertex transformations (these are covered by the VPUs). Also, this is a fixed-function pipeline, so no <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#creativity">fancy tweaking</a> or <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox/#graphics">shaders</a> either, you are stuck with a fixed shading model (e.g. Gouraud).</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/pipeline.1a430df3f9025dbee6ed7e2b3270098485970f8d9f89bd6bb87c7d9940c21d7c.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="798" height="561" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/pipeline.1a430df3f9025dbee6ed7e2b3270098485970f8d9f89bd6bb87c7d9940c21d7c.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Pipeline design of the Graphics Synthesizer</figcaption></figure><p>Looks pretty simple right? Well, let’s dive deeper to see what happens at each stage.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-3-1-pre-processing-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-3-1-pre-processing">Pre-Processing</a></li><li id="tab-3-2-rasterisation-link"><a href="#tab-3-2-rasterisation">Rasterisation</a></li><li id="tab-3-3-texturing-link"><a href="#tab-3-3-texturing">Texturing</a></li><li id="tab-3-4-testing-link"><a href="#tab-3-4-testing">Testing</a></li><li id="tab-3-5-post-processing-link"><a href="#tab-3-5-post-processing">Post-Processing</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-3-1-pre-processing"><h4 id="tab-3-1-pre-processing" class="tab-title">Pre-Processing</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/preprocessing.2b808c4e35f6c81e77a8fdf824d802b05f3cb74d80bce6893954ab80799f526a.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="818" height="431" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/preprocessing.2b808c4e35f6c81e77a8fdf824d802b05f3cb74d80bce6893954ab80799f526a.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Pre-processing stage.</figcaption></figure><p>The Emotion Engine kickstarts the Graphics Synthesizer by filling its embedded DRAM with the required materials (<strong>Texture bitmaps</strong> and <strong>Colour Lookup tables</strong>, the latter are also known as ‘CLUT’), assigning values on the GS’s registers to configure it, and finally, issuing the drawing commands (Display Lists) which instruct the GS to draw primitives (points, lines, triangles, sprites, etc) at specific locations of the screen.</p><p>Additionally, the GS will preprocess some values that will be needed for later calculations. Most notably, the <strong>Digital Differential Algorithm</strong> value, which will be used for interpolations during drawing.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-2-rasterisation">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-2-rasterisation"><h4 id="tab-3-2-rasterisation" class="tab-title">Rasterisation</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/rasterizing.5080f3cfbf3980d359f7074dc7abe80a7b1b6cb48c205dac244aa418ef594f82.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="613" height="431" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/rasterizing.5080f3cfbf3980d359f7074dc7abe80a7b1b6cb48c205dac244aa418ef594f82.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Rasterising stage.</figcaption></figure><p>Using the previous values calculated, the renderer generates pixels from the primitives. This unit can generate 8 pixels (with textures) or 16 pixels (without textures) concurrently, each pixel entry contains the following properties calculated:</p><ul><li><strong>RGBA</strong>: Corresponding to the gradient of Red, Green, Blue and Alpha (transparency).</li><li><strong>Z-value</strong>: Used for depth testing in later stages.</li><li><strong>Fog</strong>: Optional, to simulate fog in the environment.</li><li><strong>Texture properties</strong>: Contains the address of the texture in DRAM and other properties (coordinates, level of detail, filter, etc) that will be used in the next stage.</li></ul><p>It also performs <strong>Scissoring Tests</strong> to discard polygons outside the frame area (based on their X/Y values), some pixel properties are forwarded to the ‘Pixel testing’ stage for further checks. <strong>Lighting</strong> is also provided by selecting one of the two choices available, <strong>Gouraud</strong> and <strong>Flat</strong>.</p><p>The pack is then delivered to the ‘Texture mapping’ engine, but each property is operated by a specialised ‘sub-engine’, which enables to process of different properties in parallel.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-1-pre-processing">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-3-texturing">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-3-texturing"><h4 id="tab-3-3-texturing" class="tab-title">Texturing</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/textures.87835c6502a59277bd3bfd60138c7b9a8beff4fb44d867af2cca2ed3591b3ce8.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="692" height="481" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/textures.87835c6502a59277bd3bfd60138c7b9a8beff4fb44d867af2cca2ed3591b3ce8.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Texture mapping stage</figcaption></figure><p>This stage is powered by a large Pixel Unit that can compute up to 16 pixels at a time, here textures will be mapped onto the polygons (now pixels). Furthermore, fog and anti-aliasing effects are applied here.</p><p>Texture maps are fetched from DRAM in an area defined as <strong>Texture buffer</strong>, although this is interfaced by a separate area called <strong>Texture Page Buffer</strong> which seems to serve as a caching mechanism for textures. CLUTs are also mapped using this page system. Both elements are retrieved using a <strong>512-bit bus</strong>.</p><p>The pixel unit performs <strong>perspective correction</strong> to map textures onto the primitives (a great improvement considering the previous <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#tab-3-5-textures">affine mapping</a> approach). Moreover, it also provides <strong>bilinear and trilinear filtering</strong>, the latter one is used alongside mipmapped textures.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-2-rasterisation">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-4-testing">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-4-testing"><h4 id="tab-3-4-testing" class="tab-title">Testing</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/tests.51bfa7b8d3c47c02ea677b30a6999b3f051340e9199df5e32b93cac77dc30f07.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="738" height="449" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/tests.51bfa7b8d3c47c02ea677b30a6999b3f051340e9199df5e32b93cac77dc30f07.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Pixel Testing stage</figcaption></figure><p>Here certain pixels will be discarded if they don’t meet several requirements. Having said that, the following tests are carried out:</p><ul><li><strong>Alpha test</strong>: Compares the alpha value (transparency) of a pixel against the ‘standard’ value. This is because in some cases, the alpha value is required to be within a certain range or greater/less than an arbitrary value.</li><li><strong>Destination Alpha test</strong>: This checks the pixel’s alpha value again before drawing it to the frame buffer.</li><li><strong>Depth Test</strong>: Compares the pixel’s Z-value against the corresponding Z-value in the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#modern-visible-surface-determination">Z-buffer</a>. This avoids processing pixels that would be hidden behind other pixels.</li></ul><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-3-texturing">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-5-post-processing">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-5-post-processing"><h4 id="tab-3-5-post-processing" class="tab-title">Post-Processing</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/postprocessing.688bdccd66ee346f56e56bb7c219e862cb24bc8ffa29a2270453493e37ed0b67.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="723" height="431" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/gs_pipeline/postprocessing.688bdccd66ee346f56e56bb7c219e862cb24bc8ffa29a2270453493e37ed0b67.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Post-Processing stage</figcaption></figure><p>The last stage can apply some effects over our new pixels using the previous frame-buffer found in local DRAM:</p><ul><li><strong>Alpha Blending</strong>: Merges colours of the current buffer with the previous one in memory.</li><li><strong>Dithering</strong>: Large RGBA values will need to be trimmed, so dithering can be applied to soften the loss of precision.</li><li><strong>Colour Clamping</strong>: After applying operations like Alpha Blending, the new RGB value may exceed the valid range (0-255), so clamping sets the value within the range.</li><li><strong>Formatting</strong>: This converts the final frame-buffer generated in the pipeline to a format that can be stored in memory.</li></ul><p>Finally, the new frame-buffer, along with the updated Z-buffer, are written to memory using a <strong>1024-bit bus</strong>.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-4-testing">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="even-more-post-processing">Even more post-processing</h3><p>There’s a dedicated component inside the GS called <strong>Programmable CRT Controller</strong> or ‘PCRTC’ which sends the frame buffer in memory to the Video output, so you can see the frame on TV. But that’s not all: It also contains a special block called <strong>Merge Circuit</strong> that allows to alpha-blend two separate frame buffers (useful if games want to reuse the previous frame to form the new one). The resulting frame can be outputted through the video signal and/or written back to memory.</p><h3 id="better-models">Better models</h3><p>With all being said, this surely brought better designs to refresh already-famous characters.
