Shading</strong> (a term I have mentioned <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#creativity">before</a>), however, in my previous articles I explained that the GPU was mainly responsible for this. In the PS2 case, the required colour calculations are presumably done by the Emotion Engine, since the GS isn’t as flexible as other GPUs.</p><h3 id="video-output">Video Output</h3><p>As stated before, the PCRTC sends the frame buffer through the video signal. The interface can broadcast video using a wide range of formats (to work with TVs from any geographical region) <sup id="bibref:12"><a href="#bib:graphics-opl" role="doc-biblioref">[12]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li><strong>PAL</strong>: Sends up to 640x512 pixels at 50 Hz, either progressive (576p) or interlaced (576i).<ul><li>No games found in the market use 576p. While some support progressive mode, they do so in 480p mode.</li></ul></li><li><strong>NTSC</strong>: Up to 640x448 pixels at 60 Hz, either progressive (480p) or interlaced (480i).</li><li><strong>VESA</strong>: Up to 1280x1024 pixels.</li><li><strong>DTV</strong>: Up to the <em>enormous amount</em> of 720x480 pixels in progressive mode or 1920x1080 in interlaced mode.<ul><li>By tweaking the PCRTC settings, a game can also force to output in 1080p. However, this mode is undocumented and therefore subject to unpredictable behaviour.</li><li>Does that mean the PS2 can ‘display HD’? Technically… yes, but I don’t think most game studios risked the performance penalty for a format that wasn’t popularised yet.</li></ul></li></ul><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_back.90d8cb543577eee2b12c13ff6a023b820f19a749ce9bf307437bc9c594583924.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_back.90d8cb543577eee2b12c13ff6a023b820f19a749ce9bf307437bc9c594583924_hu_1d5afeee07370723.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_back.90d8cb543577eee2b12c13ff6a023b820f19a749ce9bf307437bc9c594583924_hu_1d4b857fd08c0fde.webp 800w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="800" height="568" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_back.90d8cb543577eee2b12c13ff6a023b820f19a749ce9bf307437bc9c594583924.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The right side of the console <sup id="bibref:13"><a href="#bib:photography-amos" role="doc-biblioref">[13]</a></sup>, as seen from the back. Showing A/C port, Digital audio port and AV Multi Out.</figcaption></figure><p>There’re quite a lot of modes to choose from, but it all comes down to the format adoption during the early 2000s, which narrows it down to PAL and NTSC. Also, even though PAL provided a higher resolution than NTSC, some European versions of NTSC games resorted to letterboxing to mask the unused horizontal lines and slowed down the refresh rate to fit in the 50Hz limit (I call these ‘bad ports’!).</p></div><p>The video-out port (<strong>Multi A/V</strong>) is very convenient. It carries RGB, Component, S-Video and composite. So, all the important signals are there without requiring proprietary adapters or internal modifications.</p><hr><h2 id="audio">Audio</h2><p>The new audio chip is an incremental update of the old <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#audio">SPU</a> called… <strong>SPU2</strong>! Improvements include the inclusion of <strong>2 MB of internal memory</strong> and <strong>48 channels available</strong> (two times the original amount).</p><p>The SPU2 is made of two sound processors inside, referred to as <strong>CORE0</strong> and <strong>CORE1</strong>, and runs at ~36.86 MHz. Each one processes <strong>24 channels</strong>.</p><p>Curiously enough, these are still two independent processors and to configure them, you have to alter their registers. However, Sony warned developers that both sets of registers have to be set with 1/48000 seconds of gap. If you hurry too much, the behaviour of the SPU2 becomes unpredictable!</p><p>The SPU2 inherits the same effects available from the original SPU. The memory provided is used as a ‘work area’: You can store raw waveform data and allocate extra space to process it and apply effects on it.</p><p>Finally, the chip can mix all channels to provide <strong>stereo output</strong>. Now, here is the interesting part: The SPU2 can feed itself the mixed stereo sample as new input, this enables the EE to access it (to mix it with even more audio, for instance), or keep adding more effects (such as reverb, echo and delay).</p><div class="side-by-side"><figure class="toleft"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/video_posters/goomy_noreverb.c8f9f1e5579428fad6dae2a94167adda7fc29516dfc20155c1374257585eb7ea.jpg" preload="none" width="900" height="720" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/ps2/goomy_noreverb.bf7623c844881b199d9645b3429c03b6d3866c1a114f8029add159916808896c.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Kingdom Hearts II (2005). Without reverb.</figcaption></figure><figure class="toright"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/video_posters/goomy.0a5a9e03391e94fd968da1f976015ff83d2d1a0913a5b739394cef1a036df251.jpg" preload="none" width="900" height="720" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/ps2/goomy.e54f280eaec302fad90713b37d13a88757e44d2e64fc03a9d89e56da0661002f.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Kingdom Hearts II (2005). With reverb.</figcaption></figure></div><h3 id="audio-out">Audio out</h3><p>The audio signal is outputted through two media:</p><ul><li><strong>Digital Audio</strong>: Referred to as the Sony/Philips Digital Interface or ‘S/PDIF’.</li><li><strong>Analog Audio</strong>: Goes through the digital-to-analogue converter and ends at the Multi A/V port.</li></ul><hr><h2 id="io">I/O</h2><p>Initially, the I/O of the PS2 wasn’t particularly complicated. Yet, subsequent revisions of this console completely disrupted both the internal and external designs. So, overall, this console exhibits many forms of I/O distributed across different revisions.</p><h3 id="the-special-cpu">The special CPU</h3><p>To start with, there’s a dedicated processor that arbitrates the communication between different components, this CPU is no other than the <strong>original MIPS R3000-based core</strong> found in the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#cpu">PlayStation 1</a>. This time, it’s called <strong>I/O Processor</strong> (IOP) and runs at <strong>37.5 MHz</strong> attached to a <strong>32-bit bus</strong> <sup id="bibref:14"><a href="#bib:io-buses" role="doc-biblioref">[14]</a></sup>.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/main.c21d77984fb0fbfb5d8da351b5454bccd9b27b5b39245ad399aba2b97f7be4f1.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/main.c21d77984fb0fbfb5d8da351b5454bccd9b27b5b39245ad399aba2b97f7be4f1_hu_d3a8c2641f99ee26.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/main.c21d77984fb0fbfb5d8da351b5454bccd9b27b5b39245ad399aba2b97f7be4f1_hu_e5df8612fcce15a3.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/main.c21d77984fb0fbfb5d8da351b5454bccd9b27b5b39245ad399aba2b97f7be4f1_hu_a4438d6e9941807a.webp 1783w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1783" height="1000" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/_diagrams/main.c21d77984fb0fbfb5d8da351b5454bccd9b27b5b39245ad399aba2b97f7be4f1.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Main diagram of the PlayStation 2’s architecture. Notice the I/O Processor exhibiting exclusive access to most of the I/O.</figcaption></figure><p>The IOP communicates with the Emotion Engine using a specialised I/O interface called <strong>System Interface</strong> or ‘SIF’, both endpoints use their DMA units to transfer data between each other. The IOP also comes with dedicated memory - <strong>2 MB of <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#the-offering">EDO RAM</a></strong> (just like the PS1) - used as a buffer.</p><p>All in all, this processor gives access to the front ports, DVD controller, SPU2, the BIOS ROM and the PC card slot.</p><h4 id="the-special-upgrade">The special upgrade</h4><p>Be as it may, one year after the ‘Slim’ revision arrived in 2005, the MIPS core was swapped for a <em>very unusual</em> SoC that instead houses <sup id="bibref:15"><a href="#bib:io-ppc_monitor" role="doc-biblioref">[15]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li>A <strong>PowerPC 440x5 CPU</strong>. This chip is part of the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#tab-2-1-individual-developments">streamlined PowerPC 4xx series</a> led by IBM and tailored for microcontroller applications.</li><li>An <strong>Auxiliary Processing Unit</strong> (APU), a package composed of partial MIPS R3000A circuitry (the decoder and ALU), the good-old <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#tab-2-2-geometry-transformation-engine">Geometry Transformation Engine</a> and extra registers for inter-process communication.</li><li>An <strong>Ethernet transceiver</strong> (previously sold as an external accessory).</li></ul><p>There’s also <strong>4 MB of SDRAM</strong> sitting next to the chip (2 MB more than before and ‘SDRAM’ this time).</p><p>The new package is referred to as <strong>PPC-IOP</strong> and runs at a lightning <strong>440 MHz</strong> instead. Curiously enough, the PPC CPU will still be tasked with running MIPS code <sup id="bibref:16"><a href="#bib:io-ppc_iop_discussion" role="doc-biblioref">[16]</a></sup>. This is done with the help of a MIPS emulator called <strong>DECKARD</strong> (stored in the BIOS ROM <sup id="bibref:17"><a href="#bib:io-ps2_mysteries" role="doc-biblioref">[17]</a></sup>), which makes use of the additional SDRAM and the APU to accelerate this.</p><p>As the inner workings and operating speed of PPC-IOP are considerably different from the original IOP, there’s an additional database of patches with entries for each affected game <sup id="bibref:18"><a href="#bib:io-deckard" role="doc-biblioref">[18]</a></sup>. Furthermore, DECKARD tries to approximate timings using an event handler. However, performance degrades during certain instructions <sup id="bibref:19"><a href="#bib:io-ppc_monitor" role="doc-biblioref">[19]</a></sup>. Additionally, almost 24% of SDRAM is left unused for some reason <sup id="bibref:20"><a href="#bib:io-deckard" role="doc-biblioref">[20]</a></sup>.</p><p>Considering all this, I wonder why Sony redesigned the I/O ecosystem in a way that not only it degrades performance but it also wastes all its perks. Perhaps, it was only done to reduce manufacturing costs while keeping backwards compatibility (I explain more in the next paragraphs). It’s worth mentioning that, around that time, Sony had recently <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-3/#tab-1-1-the-state-of-progress">struck a deal with IBM to build the Cell processor as well</a>.</p><h4 id="inherited-compatibility">Inherited compatibility</h4><p>For those models bundling the predecessor’s CPU, one can suspect PS1 compatibility would be part of the package. Conveniently enough, Sony did bundle a PS1 emulator (called <code>PS1DRV</code>) that loads whenever a PS1 disc is inserted. When this happens, the IOP is under-clocked to run at PS1 speed, the EE is ‘repurposed’ to emulate the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#graphics">old GPU</a> and the SPU2 is remapped to behave like the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#audio">original SPU</a>.</p><p>With PowerPC-based models, PS1DRV runs on top of DECKARD.</p><h3 id="available-interfaces">Available interfaces</h3><p>This console kept the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#front-ports">previous front ports</a> that were included in the original PlayStation, it also features a couple of ‘experimental’ interfaces that appeared very promising at first.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_front.bbcd78b8ef9b4696b02c59b8c29f7201bda73348af7e3c99cd950e8f41d09816.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_front.bbcd78b8ef9b4696b02c59b8c29f7201bda73348af7e3c99cd950e8f41d09816_hu_751bfa07eec056bf.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_front.bbcd78b8ef9b4696b02c59b8c29f7201bda73348af7e3c99cd950e8f41d09816_hu_2b624e39b86c2e8a.webp 800w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="800" height="556" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_front.bbcd78b8ef9b4696b02c59b8c29f7201bda73348af7e3c99cd950e8f41d09816.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Front of the PS2 showing common ports including Controllers and Memory Cards. Plus, the new USBs and i.Link ports <sup id="bibref:21"><a href="#bib:photography-amos" role="doc-biblioref">[21]</a></sup>.</figcaption></figure><p>The most popular additions are the <strong>two USB 1.1 ports</strong>. Its theoretical speed is 12 Mbps but that’s highly dependent on the IOP’s bandwidth (which tends to be considerably slower). Nevertheless, it was widely adopted by third-party accessories.</p><p>There were also some ‘experiments’ that didn’t last very long. For instance, the front <strong>i.Link port</strong> (also known as IEEE 1394 - or ‘FireWire’ in the Apple world). This port was used to connect two PS2s for local multiplayer, but it was removed after the third revision (presumably replaced by the ‘Network card’, more details below).</p><h4 id="the-unusual-ethernet-hdd-combo">The unusual Ethernet + HDD combo</h4><p>On the back of the console we also had a slot for <strong>PC cards</strong>. For this, you could buy the ‘Network Adaptor card’ from Sony that provides two extra interfaces:</p><ul><li>An <strong>Ethernet</strong> port, for online multiplayer.</li><li>A proprietary and external <strong>Hard Disk Drive Unit</strong> port: This was sold by Sony and packaged a typical 3.5” ATA hard drive with 40 GB of space. It enabled games to store temporary data (or permanently install themselves there) for faster load times. Just a few games used this feature, though.</li></ul><p>In later revisions, the PCMCIA port was replaced by an <strong>Expansion Bay</strong> where the 3.5” HDD could now be fitted inside the console. You had to buy first a <strong>Network adaptor</strong> which not only provided Modem and/or Ethernet ports (depending on the model) but also included the sockets to plug an ATA-66 hard disk.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/back_bay.0f66e2305d8a3e9d2e5d90c2135fedfed96261df98e782ed03b4cb31d2db6804.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/back_bay.0f66e2305d8a3e9d2e5d90c2135fedfed96261df98e782ed03b4cb31d2db6804_hu_5e24379b66c7fb23.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/back_bay.0f66e2305d8a3e9d2e5d90c2135fedfed96261df98e782ed03b4cb31d2db6804_hu_49aaaf067bd34ad8.webp 700w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="700" height="447" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/back_bay.0f66e2305d8a3e9d2e5d90c2135fedfed96261df98e782ed03b4cb31d2db6804.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Back of PS2 showing the Expansion Bay (with the cover removed) <sup id="bibref:22"><a href="#bib:photography-amos" role="doc-biblioref">[22]</a></sup>.</figcaption></figure><p>Behind the scenes, the data in the HDD is structured using a file system called ‘PFS’ <sup id="bibref:23"><a href="#bib:io-fs" role="doc-biblioref">[23]</a></sup>. Strangely, the layout doesn’t contain a partition table, just a very primitive catalogue called ‘Aligned Partition Allocation’ (APA). This may be because Sony only shipped 40 GB drives. Hence, scalability wasn’t on their list of priorities.</p><div class="side-by-side"><figure class="toleft"><a class="toleft" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/harddrive_adaptor_front.3b16514089966bf21a9a63fd2e21b2826603c39c85e2cc5d424f4af811c9e327.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/harddrive_adaptor_front.3b16514089966bf21a9a63fd2e21b2826603c39c85e2cc5d424f4af811c9e327_hu_9d1fcda024fc9872.webp 500w"><img class="title-image no-borders" alt="Image" width="500" height="365" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/harddrive_adaptor_front.3b16514089966bf21a9a63fd2e21b2826603c39c85e2cc5d424f4af811c9e327.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Network adaptor as seen from the front <sup id="bibref:24"><a href="#bib:photography-amos" role="doc-biblioref">[24]</a></sup>. This particular model provided modem and Ethernet ports.</figcaption></figure><figure class="toright"><a class="toright" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/harddrive_adaptor_back.3c6e04c3a470da2085874774b9852513bf799ccd8f286fb0126c61fe4f7f55d2.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/harddrive_adaptor_back.3c6e04c3a470da2085874774b9852513bf799ccd8f286fb0126c61fe4f7f55d2_hu_6025e8d01f065e4.webp 500w"><img class="title-image no-borders" alt="Image" width="500" height="445" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/harddrive_adaptor_back.3c6e04c3a470da2085874774b9852513bf799ccd8f286fb0126c61fe4f7f55d2.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Network adaptor as seen from the back <sup id="bibref:25"><a href="#bib:photography-amos" role="doc-biblioref">[25]</a></sup>, with a hard drive fitted.</figcaption></figure></div><p>The Ethernet transceiver within the adaptor supports transfer rates of up to 100 Mbps (12.5 MB/s). However, the <strong>observed rate is notoriously lower</strong> (down to 2 MB/s in some cases). The explanation for that is relatively simple: To achieve usable network communication, one is required to implement all the layers of the standard ‘OSI Model’; and the transceiver is just one piece of the puzzle. The rest is often delegated to the IOP (thus, done in software) but due to the IOP’s limited performance <sup id="bibref:26"><a href="#bib:io-bottleneck" role="doc-biblioref">[26]</a></sup>, this results in bottlenecks.</p><h4 id="slimming-down">Slimming down</h4><p>The Slim revision revised the whole Ethernet + HDD model: there’s no more Expansion Bay, but an Ethernet port is permanently installed on the back (particular models also included a Modem).</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_slim_back.cf86a86f76a569ea7b55e93f810c235b803994138cecdc239da1b5fb51a28408.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_slim_back.cf86a86f76a569ea7b55e93f810c235b803994138cecdc239da1b5fb51a28408_hu_2db65df54e9be65d.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_slim_back.cf86a86f76a569ea7b55e93f810c235b803994138cecdc239da1b5fb51a28408_hu_2fd0e7d11008f498.webp 800w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="800" height="256" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/ps2_slim_back.cf86a86f76a569ea7b55e93f810c235b803994138cecdc239da1b5fb51a28408.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Back of the slim model, showing a fixed Ethernet port.</figcaption></figure><p>In addition to that, the new revision added a new <strong>infrared sensor</strong>, to be used with a Sony-branded remote controller (sold separately).</p><h3 id="interactive-accessories">Interactive accessories</h3><p>The new version of their controller, the <strong>DualShock 2</strong>, is a slightly improved version of DualShock.</p><div class="side-by-side"><figure class="toleft"><a class="toleft" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/dualshock2.282d39495166ea2e6292eca7855f85c16e7382e582cd7500e171e4989b1c0748.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/dualshock2.282d39495166ea2e6292eca7855f85c16e7382e582cd7500e171e4989b1c0748_hu_15e4881efc88f80.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/dualshock2.282d39495166ea2e6292eca7855f85c16e7382e582cd7500e171e4989b1c0748_hu_9c2ba46e72f65448.webp 800w"><img class="title-image no-borders" alt="Image" width="800" height="642" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/dualshock2.282d39495166ea2e6292eca7855f85c16e7382e582cd7500e171e4989b1c0748.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The DualShock 2 controller <sup id="bibref:27"><a href="#bib:photography-amos" role="doc-biblioref">[27]</a></sup>.</figcaption></figure><figure class="toright"><a class="toright" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/memorycard.d428f4311e3a13e6493b42c25a8aa6a86a0ee0390f9282bf2a2bca392906fb0c.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/memorycard.d428f4311e3a13e6493b42c25a8aa6a86a0ee0390f9282bf2a2bca392906fb0c_hu_f1c317ce2a69819f.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/memorycard.d428f4311e3a13e6493b42c25a8aa6a86a0ee0390f9282bf2a2bca392906fb0c_hu_1aa0990c6f5b1c8e.webp 800w"><img class="title-image no-borders" alt="Image" width="800" height="586" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/photos/memorycard.d428f4311e3a13e6493b42c25a8aa6a86a0ee0390f9282bf2a2bca392906fb0c.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">An official Memory Card (8 MB model) <sup id="bibref:28"><a href="#bib:photography-amos" role="doc-biblioref">[28]</a></sup>.</figcaption></figure></div><p>During the days of the original PlayStation, multiple revisions of the original controller were released featuring different features (and also bringing fragmentation to the market). Now, for the benefit of developers, there was a single controller that unified all the previous properties.</p><p>Compared to the original DualShock, the new version features a slight redesign, it includes two analogue sticks and two vibration motors for richer input and feedback, respectively.</p><p>Next to the controller slot is the <strong>Memory Card</strong> one, now compatible with PS1 and PS2 cards. The latter cards embed extra circuitry for security purposes referred to as <strong>MagicGate</strong>, which enables games to restrict data transfers between different memory cards. The IOP takes care of encrypting and decrypting the content, and it does so with the help of the MagicGate chipset (found inside the Memory Card) and the DVD drive, the latter bundles the encryption keys.</p><p>Some third-party Memory Cards didn’t support MagicGate, however.</p><hr><h2 id="operating-system">Operating System</h2><p>There’s a <strong>4 MB ROM</strong> chip fitted on the motherboard, this stores a great amount of code used to load a shell menu (that the users can interact with) but it also provides system calls to simplify I/O access <sup id="bibref:29"><a href="#bib:cpu-rockin" role="doc-biblioref">[29]</a></sup> (which games rely on).</p><div class="tabs nested centered-container"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-2-1-boot-animation-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-2-1-boot-animation">Boot animation</a></li><li id="nestedtab-2-2-valid-disc-link"><a href="#nestedtab-2-2-valid-disc">Valid disc</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-2-1-boot-animation"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/animated.72945211f44eb65a6c236fbb9fe875bd0bf3f79eed8f0e65103b4b8abedeef2f.jpg"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="640" height="448" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/animated.72945211f44eb65a6c236fbb9fe875bd0bf3f79eed8f0e65103b4b8abedeef2f.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Splash animation after turning on the console.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-2-2-valid-disc"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/game_splash.f251c2bbc47957aaa37328f26590eee36c7cc48aca5f484b712aee77bf2bbfad.jpg"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="640" height="448" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/game_splash.f251c2bbc47957aaa37328f26590eee36c7cc48aca5f484b712aee77bf2bbfad.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">PS2 logo showing after a valid PS2 game is inserted.</figcaption></figure></div><p>Upon receiving power, both the MIPS R5900 and the IOP will start at address <code>0xBFC00000</code> (that’s the signature reset vector for all MIPS CPUs). To handle the expected conflicts, however, the respective code stored in that address (pointing to the BIOS ROM) will make each CPU branch at a different location based on its identifier.</p><p>In the case of the R5900, the CPU will follow these steps <sup id="bibref:30"><a href="#bib:cpu-rockin" role="doc-biblioref">[30]</a></sup>:</p><ol style="list-style-type:decimal"><li>Initialise the hardware.</li><li>Load the <strong>Kernel</strong> from ROM into RAM. Once loaded, the Kernel will provide a layer of abstraction to applications (mostly games) to interact with the hardware. Additionally, it also exposes a multi-threading API (cooperative and priority-based).</li><li>The Kernel loads <code>EELOAD</code>, a kernel module which, in turn, bootstraps <code>OSDSYS</code>. The latter is the program that displays the splash animation and the shell menu.</li></ol><p>On the other side, the IOP will be initialising part of its hardware and then load multiple <strong>modules</strong>, these enable the IOP to access the hardware of this console. Once finished, the IOP will be put in a ‘waiting for command’ state.</p><p>It’s worth pointing out that the use of modules allows Sony to release new hardware revisions of the PS2 without changing the IOP (until they did), thereby lowering some production costs in the process.</p><h3 id="interactive-shell">Interactive shell</h3><p>The functionality of the PS2 shell is pretty much in pace with the other 6th-generation consoles.</p><div class="tabs nested centered-container"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-3-1-menu-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-3-1-menu">Menu</a></li><li id="nestedtab-3-2-browser-link"><a href="#nestedtab-3-2-browser">Browser</a></li><li id="nestedtab-3-3-saves-link"><a href="#nestedtab-3-3-saves">Saves</a></li><li id="nestedtab-3-4-editor-link"><a href="#nestedtab-3-4-editor">Editor</a></li><li id="nestedtab-3-5-options-link"><a href="#nestedtab-3-5-options">Options</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-3-1-menu"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/menu.dc34d3f7df1dfdecd2b8d161baf4dc0df949fc8bccf4053c1af018445e514341.jpg"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="640" height="448" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/menu.dc34d3f7df1dfdecd2b8d161baf4dc0df949fc8bccf4053c1af018445e514341.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Initial menu. Appears when there’s no disc inserted.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-3-2-browser"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/mem_list.3290e6b3a5adc2eeef517803236b3b2612cff1b8d19b540b4017e97f615b665c.jpg"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="640" height="448" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/mem_list.3290e6b3a5adc2eeef517803236b3b2612cff1b8d19b540b4017e97f615b665c.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Memory Card browser.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-3-3-saves"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/save_list.b5d3183363f0c9525caf4c9ebc5d04ba1687f5860a8a0534119b835d444baf81.jpg"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="640" height="448" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/save_list.b5d3183363f0c9525caf4c9ebc5d04ba1687f5860a8a0534119b835d444baf81.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Saves browser. It shows up after selecting a memory card.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-3-4-editor"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/save_editor.8a4443cdbecf5013439375d6bf546897a35942c8e57904944c4dd23f8d5cf57e.jpg"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="640" height="448" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/save_editor.8a4443cdbecf5013439375d6bf546897a35942c8e57904944c4dd23f8d5cf57e.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Save editor, displayed after selecting a save.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-3-5-options"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/options.c86de317d64a6dd77a3685f3a70d5cd77737b1d85a14ae2e31e406c94b75b86a.jpg"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="640" height="448" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/options.c86de317d64a6dd77a3685f3a70d5cd77737b1d85a14ae2e31e406c94b75b86a.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">System Configuration.</figcaption></figure></div><p>The shell is composed of multiple user interfaces for managing typical operations, like manipulating the save data stored in the memory card or altering the clock. It also provides some advanced options, like changing the current video mode.</p><h3 id="updatability">Updatability</h3><p>The BIOS is indeed stored within read-only memory, but that didn’t stop Sony from amending it after leaving the factory. You see, behind the scenes, the BIOS left two doors open for future alterations:</p><ul><li>Applications (games and <code>OSDSYS</code>) can <strong>monkey patch the kernel routines at runtime</strong> <sup id="bibref:31"><a href="#bib:operating_system-kpatch" role="doc-biblioref">[31]</a></sup>. Both the official SDK and the unofficial ‘ps2sdk’ made extensive use of this, as Sony’s engineers subsequently discovered their Kernel to be riddled with bugs (<em>pun intended</em>).</li><li><strong><code>EELOAD</code> will look for an updated <code>OSDSYS</code> binary stored in the Memory Card and/or the HDD</strong> <sup id="bibref:32"><a href="#bib:operating_system-israelson" role="doc-biblioref">[32]</a></sup>. Sony relied on this to add a DVD movie player and HDD support, as none of these drivers were bundled in the earlier revisions of this console.<ul><li>These updates were distributed in installation discs that came with the console or the HDD kit (part of the Final Fantasy XI box set).</li><li>Unlike the Kernel, which has to be backwards compatible with old SDKs, follow-up revisions of the console shipped previous updates in the BIOS ROM.</li><li>To control distribution, binaries must be signed with <strong>Data Encryption Standard</strong> (DES) <sup id="bibref:33"><a href="#bib:operating_system-kelftool" role="doc-biblioref">[33]</a></sup>, a symmetric encryption system, using keys only known by Sony (in theory). Additionally, the binaries must be stored in a storage device with MagicGate support.</li></ul></li></ul><p>In any case, Sony eventually removed the second method in late PS2 models (with a BIOS version <code>2.30</code>). I presume Sony wasn’t planning any more updates and this just added up to the attack surface.</p><hr><h2 id="games">Games</h2><p>It is unprecedented the level of popularity this system achieved during the noughties, at the end of its lifespan (2013, after 13 years!) the game library was filled with 1850 titles <sup id="bibref:34"><a href="#bib:games-antista" role="doc-biblioref">[34]</a></sup>.</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/mr_moskeeto.4389bc5124e7c6d203234780d30e54eadb0264df16d35531c7afd4483acffdbf.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/mr_moskeeto.4389bc5124e7c6d203234780d30e54eadb0264df16d35531c7afd4483acffdbf_hu_8b3c047078658455.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/mr_moskeeto.4389bc5124e7c6d203234780d30e54eadb0264df16d35531c7afd4483acffdbf_hu_13e50f2ad5f6ba04.webp 760w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="760" height="498" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/mr_moskeeto.4389bc5124e7c6d203234780d30e54eadb0264df16d35531c7afd4483acffdbf.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Mr Moskeeto (2001). Whenever someone argues about the abundance of PS2 games, I remember this one.</figcaption></figure><p>What happened here is really impressive. The PS2 doesn’t have a ‘programmer-friendly’ architecture, (as seen from the perspective of a PC programmer) yet with such an amount of games developed, I too wonder if there were more factors involved (such as ‘licensing reliefs’, low distribution costs, cost of development, small form factor and what not).</p></div><h3 id="development-ecosystem">Development ecosystem</h3><p>Sony provided the hardware and software to assist game development.</p><p>On the software side, there was the <strong>PlayStation 2 SDK</strong> which included <sup id="bibref:35"><a href="#bib:games-sdkkit" role="doc-biblioref">[35]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li>The Emotion Engine toolchain: A set of <strong>C</strong> and <strong>C++</strong> compilers, assemblers, linkers and debuggers used to control each element of the EE. The main CPU was mainly programmed using C/C++, however, performance-critical components like the vector units were programmed using assembly (microcode/macrocode) instead.<ul><li>The pack also included an ‘Emotion Engine simulator’ which could roughly test out the code without sending it to the real hardware, although the simulator wasn’t as accurate as the physical EE chip.</li><li>All of these tools worked on Linux, Solaris and Windows. The latter variant ran under the Cygnus environment.</li></ul></li><li>Low-level libraries: Interfaced many system functions (using BIOS calls).</li><li>‘Analysis’ tools to profile performance usage.</li><li>Additional tools to connect with the official development hardware.</li></ul><p>On the hardware side, Sony provided studios with dedicated hardware to run and debug games in-house. The initial devkits were bare boards stacked together to replicate the unreleased hardware of the PS2. Later kits (named <strong>Development Tool</strong>), had a more presentable appearance, enhanced I/O and combined workstation hardware (running RedHat 5.2) with PS2 hardware to build and deploy the game in the same case <sup id="bibref:36"><a href="#bib:games-devkit" role="doc-biblioref">[36]</a></sup>.</p><p>The combination of the Devkit, the official SDK and CodeWarrior (a famous IDE) was one of the most popular setups.</p><h3 id="medium">Medium</h3><p>The disc drive can read both DVDs and CDs, so games could be distributed using either format, but for obvious reasons, you will find most titles in DVD format.</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/kh2_box.2054a1f740895a75f23b07557852c931e9c4418343089913c7c3312b06e1bffe.jpeg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/kh2_box.2054a1f740895a75f23b07557852c931e9c4418343089913c7c3312b06e1bffe_hu_15de2dfb37ade764.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/kh2_box.2054a1f740895a75f23b07557852c931e9c4418343089913c7c3312b06e1bffe_hu_8a828fbcd689d851.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/kh2_box.2054a1f740895a75f23b07557852c931e9c4418343089913c7c3312b06e1bffe_hu_32fe65c8306b2800.webp 1111w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1111" height="841" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/kh2_box.2054a1f740895a75f23b07557852c931e9c4418343089913c7c3312b06e1bffe.jpeg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Kingdom Hearts II (2005). Typical retail game box and disc.</figcaption></figure><p>DVDs can hold up <strong>4.7 GB</strong> of data in the case of <strong>DVD-5</strong> (the most common ‘sub-format’) or <strong>8.5 GB</strong> in the case of <strong>DVD-9</strong> (dual-layer version, less common) <sup id="bibref:37"><a href="#bib:games-dvd" role="doc-biblioref">[37]</a></sup>. There’s actually a third format, <strong>DVD-10</strong>, which is double-sided but no commercial games ever made use of it.</p><p>Due to the type of medium used, not only games could be played, but also movies. Now, this requires a decoder to be able to read the DVD movie format, and for that, the PS2 initially included the required bits installed in the memory card (after all, the card is just a storage medium) but later models came with the DVD software pre-installed in the BIOS ROM.</p></div><p>In terms of speed, CD-ROMs are read at 24x speed (so 3.6 MB/s) and DVD-ROMs are read at 4x speed (5.28 MB/s) <sup id="bibref:38"><a href="#bib:games-transfer" role="doc-biblioref">[38]</a></sup>.</p><h3 id="network-service">Network service</h3><p>As you have seen, the networking features of these consoles weren’t standardised until later revisions, which arrived four years later after the first release. Similarly, game studios were in charge of providing the necessary infrastructure if they decided to provide online services (like multiplayer). In later years, Sony deployed the <strong>Dynamic Network Authentication System</strong> or ‘DNAS’, it wasn’t an online server, but an authentication system to prevent pirated games from connecting online.</p><h3 id="an-unusual-kind-of-game">An unusual kind of game</h3><p>Apart from all these games with their <em>fancy graphics</em>, Sony released a Linux distribution based on ‘Kondara’ (which is in turn based on Red Hat 6) available in two DVDs (the first disc is called ‘Runtime Environment’ and the second one is called ‘Software Packages’) along with a VGA adapter, USB Keyboard and Mouse; plus some developer manuals. The pack was known as <strong>Linux Kit</strong> and you could run the OS by booting the first DVD and then proceed like any <em>old-school</em> Linux environment. You obviously needed a Hard drive fitted in the console to install the Linux distro. Once installed, the first DVD was always required to boot this OS.</p><p>Linux Kit included compilers targeting the EE (gcc 2.95.2 with glibc 2.2.2) and assemblers targeting the vector units, along with a window system (XFree86 3.3.6) ‘accelerated’ in the Graphics Synthesizer <sup id="bibref:39"><a href="#bib:games-linux" role="doc-biblioref">[39]</a></sup>. Overall, this sounds like an interesting environment. In fact, one of the research papers I read to write this article was carried out using this setup.</p><hr><h2 id="anti-piracy-and-homebrew">Anti-Piracy and Homebrew</h2><p>There’s quite a lot to talk about here, so let’s start with the DVD reader, shall we?</p><h3 id="dvd-copy-protection">DVD copy protection</h3><p>This area was particularly concerning for game studios, since this console used a very affordable disc format to distribute games. Thus, the risk of piracy was high.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/rsod.eb5e045c54cdfecc4e91c0b007ddd84f7dff43602db0c9df1ba5ad2a73792d6f.jpg"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="640" height="448" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/ps2/bios/rsod.eb5e045c54cdfecc4e91c0b007ddd84f7dff43602db0c9df1ba5ad2a73792d6f.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">This error screen could appear if the drive is faulty… or a pirated copy was inserted.</figcaption></figure><p>When the OS loads a game, it does so by sending specific commands to the DVD reader. The commands specifically used to read the content of a game behave very differently from standard DVD commands (i.e. to read a DVD movie). It turns out authorised games contain an out-of-reach ‘map file’ in the inner section of the disc that indexes the filesystem by name, position and size. When the DVD is asked to read a game disc, it will always navigate through the disc using the map file, meaning that a pirated copy of a game, which could not include the map file, will be impossible to read.</p><p>This was complemented by a region lock system that prevented imported games from working in a console from a different region.</p><h3 id="circumventing-protections">Circumventing protections</h3><p>Having explained the most critical parts of this console, let’s take a look at multiple methods discovered (and commercialised) that defeated the protection mechanisms.</p><h4 id="attacking-the-dvd-drive">Attacking the DVD drive</h4><p>As soon as the PS2 reached the stores, multiple third-party products appeared with the promise to ‘unlock’ the DVD drive. With no sign to support Homebrew (outside the Linux solution), piracy was the biggest beneficiary.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-4-1-modchips-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-4-1-modchips">Modchips</a></li><li id="tab-4-2-cheats-link"><a href="#tab-4-2-cheats">Cheats</a></li><li id="tab-4-3-disc-swapping-link"><a href="#tab-4-3-disc-swapping">Disc swapping</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-4-1-modchips"><h5 id="tab-4-1-modchips" class="tab-title">Modchips</h5><p>As with any other console of its generation (and previous ones) using disc-based systems, it was a matter of time before third-party companies reversed-engineered the DVD subsystem. The goal here was to find a usable exploit that could force the driver to navigate through the file system without needing an out-of-reach map file.</p><p>This eventually materialised in the form of <strong>modchips</strong>, which lifted the copy protection checks and region-locking restrictions as well.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-4-2-cheats">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-4-2-cheats"><h5 id="tab-4-2-cheats" class="tab-title">Cheats</h5><p>Along with the modchips, which required soldering skills to install them, unauthorised but ‘genuine’ discs appeared in the market. These patched the Kernel to remove the region protection and use in-game cheats.</p><p>Most importantly, ‘cheat discs’ had the advantage of not requiring any modification on the console. I guess the best example to mention is <em>CodeBreaker</em>.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-4-1-modchips">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-4-3-disc-swapping">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-4-3-disc-swapping"><h5 id="tab-4-3-disc-swapping" class="tab-title">Disc swapping</h5><p>In the middle of the latest advancements, yet another trick appeared. This time, exploiting the reader’s handling of faulty sectors. <strong>Swap Magic</strong> looked like another ‘genuine’ disc, but its ‘game’ tells the DVD to read a non-existent executable found on a deliberately faulty sector, halting the driver altogether <sup id="bibref:40"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-hacking" role="doc-biblioref">[40]</a></sup>. This window of opportunity allowed users to swap the disc for a non-genuine one. Then Swap Magic, still loaded in memory, bootstrapped the main executable of the new disc, loading a real game at the end. All of this is carried out while the driver is still thinking a genuine disc is inserted.</p><p>This doesn’t necessarily require altering the console. However, depending on the model, the external case of the PS2 will have to be tampered with to block the eject sensors of the drive. In some models, placing pieces of cotton in certain places was part of the walkthrough.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-4-2-cheats">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h4 id="departing-from-modchips">Departing from modchips</h4><p>As time passed, more research was gathered and shared about this console. Consequently, new and more sophisticated discoveries led to a new wave of development that didn’t rely on external hardware anymore, at least primarily. Furthermore, piracy wasn’t the main focus anymore. Instead, the ability to run third-party programs without the approval of Sony (called <strong>Homebrew</strong>) quickly topped the goals chart.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-5-1-independence-overflow-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-5-1-independence-overflow">Independence overflow</a></li><li id="tab-5-2-the-signature-exploit-link"><a href="#tab-5-2-the-signature-exploit">The signature exploit</a></li><li id="tab-5-3-the-universal-solution-link"><a href="#tab-5-3-the-universal-solution">The universal solution</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-5-1-independence-overflow"><h4 id="tab-5-1-independence-overflow" class="tab-title">Independence overflow</h4><p>The PS2 stores a database file called <code>TITLE.DB</code> in MemoryCard which contains information used to optimise the emulation of PS1 games <sup id="bibref:41"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-grand" role="doc-biblioref">[41]</a></sup>. When a PS1 game is inserted, the OS fetches the database file and loads the whole file in memory at a fixed address (<em>strike one</em>). The information parser is implemented using <strong><code>strncpy()</code></strong>, a function in C that copies strings (chains of characters) from one place to another.</p><p>For people familiar with C, you probably guessed where I’m going. The thing is that <code>strncpy()</code> doesn’t know how long is a string, so unless it’s terminated (by placing <code>\0</code> at the end of the chain) the copy goes on ‘forever’ (with unpredictable results!). Luckily, this function contains an optional parameter that specifies the maximum number of bytes to be copied, protecting the copy from buffer overflows. As ludicrous as it may seem, <strong>Sony didn’t use this parameter</strong>, even though each database entry has a fixed size of 256 bytes (<em>strike two</em>).</p><p>Upon closer inspection in RAM, <code>TITLE.DB</code> happens to be copied <strong>next to a saved register</strong>, <code>$ra</code>, which states the address to return after the current function being executed finishes (<em>strike three</em>), leading up to <strong>The independence exploit</strong> <sup id="bibref:42"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-independence" role="doc-biblioref">[42]</a></sup>: Craft a <code>TITLE.DB</code> with a large string, embed an executable in it and design that string so <code>$ra</code> will be overridden to point to the executable. If you manage to upload that file to your Memory Card (through another exploit or a PC USB adapter) you got yourself a simple <strong>Homebrew launcher</strong>.</p><p>The discovery was published in 2003. Consequently, with the slim revision, Sony shipped a new BIOS ROM revision that patched this exploit. Curiously enough, it wasn’t the last <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#the-fall-of-encryption">blunder</a> that exposed clumsy code.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-5-2-the-signature-exploit">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-5-2-the-signature-exploit"><h4 id="tab-5-2-the-signature-exploit" class="tab-title">The signature exploit</h4><p>In November 2007, a hacking group started selling <strong>Memor32</strong> <sup id="bibref:43"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-fmcb" role="doc-biblioref">[43]</a></sup>, just another typical third-party Memory Card, except that for some reason it housed an <strong>FPGA</strong> and a <strong>USB port</strong>. It wasn’t until a firmware called <strong>Memento</strong> appeared on internet forums that the real nature of Memor32 became clear: To run unauthorised executables from the memory card, just like the Independence exploit.</p><p>The implementation of Memento relied on a flaw in the way the signature of the DVD player is checked. It was discovered that, while binaries have to be signed using Sony’s keys, <strong>the integrity of the binary is not checked</strong>. So, anyone could replace the executable code with something else (that still fits in the same space) and the operating system will happily run it. The Memento firmware used this exploit to disguise its payload within the DVD player, and bundles a couple of utilities that would allow users to load games (either from the disc drive or the HDD).</p><p>However, the popularity of Memor32 and Memento was soon displaced once a free (and initially open-source) alternative arrived: <strong>FreeMCBoot</strong>.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-5-1-independence-overflow">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-5-3-the-universal-solution">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-5-3-the-universal-solution"><h4 id="tab-5-3-the-universal-solution" class="tab-title">The universal solution</h4><p>Once Memento got reverse-engineered, an alternative that didn’t require Memor32 appeared on the internet. <strong>FreeMCBoot</strong> exploited the same vulnerability except it could be <strong>installed on any MagicGate Memory Card</strong>. The only drawback is that another exploit (e.g. disc swapping) was still required to bootstrap the installer.</p><p>Interestingly enough, FreeMCBoot’s user interface borrows assets from <code>OSDSYS</code>, thereby providing a familiar menu to launch other Homebrew. It also patches the Kernel to add APIs to access mass storage devices in the USB 1.1 ports, something many homebrew apps relied on to locate additional files.</p><p>Additionally, the installer provides two options: to install only the files needed for the current console, or install a global setup for all PS2 variants. Curiously enough, the latter option was challenging to accomplish <sup id="bibref:44"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-fmcb" role="doc-biblioref">[44]</a></sup>. Initially, the installer would fiddle with the partition table of the Memory Card to avoid running out of space, something that wasn’t particularly safe.</p><p>As luck would have it, in 2011, the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-3/#os-security-hierarchy">security system</a> of the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-3/">PlayStation 3</a> had just been <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-3/#tab-9-4-the-fall-of-encryption">compromised</a>, exposing many secrets hidden within. Among others, a collection of MagicGate keys globaly used for <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-3/#backwards-compatibility">PS2 backwards compatibility</a>. From then on, it was no longer needed to resort to the limited DVD binary signature trick to craft PS2 executables. And so, since version <code>1.8b</code>, FreeMCBoot has maintained its position as the safest and most popular method for running any type of Homebrew on a PlayStation 2.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-5-2-the-signature-exploit">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="follow-up-developments">Follow-up developments</h3><p>Once the avenue for running Homebrew became more accessible, progress continued in the form of polishing previous exploits and developing Homebrew applications. Some of the latter ultimately facilitated piracy-related functionality, but they also expanded the limited capabilities of the operating system (i.e. by providing patches on games), I guess it ultimately depended on the intentions of its users.</p><p>To name a few notable examples of homebrew-related developments:</p><ul><li><strong>FreeHDBoot</strong>: A variant of FreeMCBoot that instead installs on the HDD, where the system will also try to boot from.</li><li><strong>ps2sdk</strong> by the ps2dev group <sup id="bibref:45"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-ps2sdk" role="doc-biblioref">[45]</a></sup>: The defacto unofficial SDK for writing PS2 Homebrew without risk of copyright infringement. The project dates back to 2000, when it was only found in the form of loose libraries for accessing particular components <sup id="bibref:46"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-ps2sdk_history" role="doc-biblioref">[46]</a></sup> and over time unified into a single package for the benefit of Homebrew developers.</li><li><strong>LaunchELF</strong> by multiple authors <sup id="bibref:47"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-launchelf" role="doc-biblioref">[47]</a></sup>: A file manager with extra utilities. It was then continued as ‘uLaunchELF’ and, finally, ‘wLaunchELF’.</li><li><strong>Open USB Loader</strong> (OPL) by multiple authors <sup id="bibref:48"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-opl" role="doc-biblioref">[48]</a></sup>: Enables to boot disc images from multiple sources (HDD, USB, i.Link and even SMB and NMB over Ethernet) with patching capabilities.</li><li><strong>ESR</strong> by ffgriever <sup id="bibref:49"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-esr" role="doc-biblioref">[49]</a></sup>: Originally called ‘Vast CDVDV’, this is an application that tricks the whole system (including the DVD drive) into running a burned copy of a game without hardware modification. The original game content must be patched to disguise itself as a DVD movie (so the DVD drive doesn’t reject it), while ESR takes control of the Emotion Engine and IOP to redirect execution to the actual game.</li></ul><p>Later years will also see new exploits uncovered:</p><ul><li><strong>Fortuna</strong> by krat0s <sup id="bibref:50"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-fortuna" role="doc-biblioref">[50]</a></sup>: An alternative Homebrew launcher published in 2019 that relies on a completely different exploit. This time, it’s a buffer overflow in the icon parser of the saves manager (part of <code>OSDSYS</code>) <sup id="bibref:51"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-opentuna" role="doc-biblioref">[51]</a></sup>. Its main advantage is compatibility with late PS2 models that removed support for external <code>OSDSYS</code> updates (thus, incompatible with FreeMCBoot).</li><li><strong>OpenTuna</strong> by alexparrado <sup id="bibref:52"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-opentuna" role="doc-biblioref">[52]</a></sup>: An open-source alternative to Fortuna originated from reverse-engineering the latter.</li><li><strong>FreeDVDBoot</strong> by cturt <sup id="bibref:53"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-freedvdboot" role="doc-biblioref">[53]</a></sup>: A new vulnerability published in 2020. It consists of a new buffer overflow in the DVD player that can be exploited to perform arbitrary code execution. Users only need to burn a DVD with FreeDVDBoot to execute any binary they want, including the FreeMCBoot installer or even ESR (Sony was very lucky that this wasn’t discovered many years earlier! <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/dreamcast/#defeating-it">as others weren’t</a>).</li></ul><hr><h2 id="thats-all-folks">That’s all folks</h2><p>Congratulations and thank you for reaching the end of the article!
